headline_hi: बच्चों को दी शिक्षा की नई राह
headline_en: Provided children with a new path to education
summary_en: A very inspiring story has emerged from Madhya Pradesh. Here, 32-year-old Shruti Shrivastava has brought a big change in education. She had failed to clear the UPSC exam six times. But instead of giving up, she kept full faith in herself. At the age of 30, she started the Sashaktikaran Foundation. The foundation's Project Neev gave new hope to 900 rural children. This initiative has spread across 10 government schools and 9 hostels in 6 districts. Children are now easily learning math and English using tablets with games. Fifth-grade student Jamna Prasad now eagerly plays the monkey game. Along with this, 30 local women have gained employment as Shiksha Saathis. Shruti has proven that with true dedication, every path becomes easy.

lead.title: After 6 Failed UPSC Attempts, She Restarted at 30 to Help 900 Rural Kids Catch Up in Maths & English
lead.summary: “I did not like going to school. The teachers taught us, but sometimes they also scolded and hit us. I never really felt interested in learning,” recalls nine-year-old Jamna Prasad. Growing up in Bankhedi village in Madhya Pradesh, school was never a place he looked forward to . With teachers juggling several classes at once, asking questions or learning at his own pace was rarely possible. Today, the Class 5 student eagerly waits for his turn with a tablet that teaches through games. He can now read the alphabet, solve addition and subtraction, and dreams of wearing a police uniform one day. “I enjoy learning with my friends,” he says. “The Monkey Game is my favourite. Now I understand my studies much better.” Across six districts of Madhya Pradesh, children who struggled with basic lessons are beginning to learn differently. Behind the change is 32-year-old Shruti Shrivastava, who once imagined serving from inside a government office. Today, as founder-director of Sashaktikaran Foundation, she oversees Project Neev, which has reached around 900 children across 10 government schools and nine residential hostels, while creating livelihoods for 30 rural women as Shiksha Saathis. Looking back, she says her purpose did not change. Only the path did. When the IAS dream came to an end  Shruti grew up across several towns in Madhya Pradesh because of her parents’ transferable government jobs, exposing her early to inequalities in education and opportunity. headline_hi: सोलर बिजली से मिली लोगों को राहत
headline_en: Solar power brought relief to people
summary_en: Power outages are common during storms in the US state of Louisiana. Hurricane Francine in the year 2024 plunged New Orleans into darkness. In such difficult times, Pastor Shawn Anglim opened the doors of his church. This church had a special setup of solar panels and backup batteries. By afternoon, more than 100 people arrived there to find relief. People enjoyed air conditioning there and also charged their medical devices. Twenty such Community Lighthouse centers are now operating in Louisiana. These include 14 centers in New Orleans and 6 surrounding centers. This solar initiative began after the major Hurricane Ida in 2021. At that time, prolonged power cuts and intense heat had caused severe distress. Now, this network has become a safe refuge for people in times of crisis.

lead.title: The Spark: The ‘Community Lighthouses’ Where Neighbors Help Neighbors
lead.summary: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue Neighborhood hubs for emergency electricity DIY communal internet infrastructure An all-volunteer ambulance service Neighbors light the way As Hurricane Francine plunged New Orleans into yet another extended blackout in 2024, Pastor Shawn Anglim opened up the First Grace United Methodist Church and turned on the lights. “By the afternoon it was packed,” he says. “More than 100 people in air conditioning, charging up medical devices, charging up their phones.” Anglim’s church is one of a growing network of Community Lighthouses — churches, synagogues, mosques and community centers in Louisiana that have set up solar panels and batteries to provide their communities with electricity in times of need. There are now 14 Community Lighthouses in New Orleans and an additional six in broader Louisiana. Courtesy of Together New Orleans The idea was born in 2021, after Hurricane Ida caused the most extensive power outage in Louisiana’s history , leaving parts of New Orleans with no power for 12 days . The storm was followed by a heatwave, leading to at least 11 heat-related deaths as people were unable to use air conditioning in their homes. “That really gave us all pause, you know, what can we do about that?” says Anglim. headline_hi: पहाड़ों में दौड़ी पहली सोलर ट्रेन
headline_en: First solar train ran in the mountains
summary_en: A unique train powered by solar energy is running in the mountains of Argentina. This is Latin America's first solar-powered passenger train. This train connects six towns in the beautiful valleys of Humahuaca. Train service has returned to this 42-kilometer-long route after 30 years. This two-coach train is fitted with six lithium batteries. These batteries are quickly charged with solar energy from Jujuy province. Once fully charged, this train runs for up to 120 kilometers. Fast charging facilities are available for it at Volcán and Purmamarca stations. By braking on downhill slopes in the mountains, this train also generates additional electricity. This smoke-free and diesel-free journey has become a boon for the environment. For locals and tourists, this journey has now become extremely convenient.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: How Argentina’s battery-powered Tren Solar is recharging an ancient Andean route
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There are places where the land itself seems to generate energy. The Quebrada de Humahuaca in Jujuy province, in Argentina’s far northwest, is one of them. At altitude, in clear desert air, the valley gets solar radiation that would be hard to match anywhere at lower elevation. For most of its history, that energy was just weather. Now it runs a train. The Tren Solar de la Quebrada , Latin America’s first solar-powered railway, has been running since June 2024, carrying passengers 42 kilometers (26 miles) through the Andes between six towns. The route passes through a UNESCO World Heritage valley that people have crossed for thousands of years. A route through the Andes for millennia The Quebrada de Humahuaca is not a valley that has been waiting for discovery. Pre-Inca peoples used it as a trading route. Spanish colonial roads followed the same path centuries later. Today, it connects communities between Volcán in the south and Tilcara in the north, places that had passenger rail for much of the 20th century, and then didn’t. Rail disappeared from the valley around 30 years ago. The Tren Solar brought it back, minus the diesel. How the battery system works without a grid Six batteries and two fast-charging stops The train does not generate electricity from panels on its roof. Rather, the two-car train runs on six lithium batteries , charged with solar energy from Jujuy province. That gives it a range of 100 to 120 kilometers (62 to 75 miles), more than twice its current route length. Fast-charging stations at Volcán and Purmamarca allow top-ups along the way; a third is planned for the northern terminus at Tilcara. headline_hi: ज़रूरतमंद छात्रों को मिला सुरक्षित आशियाना
headline_en: Students in need found a safe shelter
summary_en: Being homeless during college studies is a very big challenge. The Dax Program has taken a great initiative to overcome this problem. A new hostel has opened for homeless students in the US city of Denver. Here, students in need get a safe place to stay for up to two years. A former student named Nykia Harrell shared her past ordeal. While studying in Chicago, she had no place to live or eat. Her life changed completely after joining Dax on a therapist's advice. In this historic Denver building, 15 students will live comfortably together. The organization has provided a safe roof to nearly 500 students so far. Eleven of its centers are running across several major cities, including Chicago and New York. Now, these young people will be able to complete their college degrees without any worries.

lead.title: A Place to Sleep for Denver’s Homeless College Students
lead.summary: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters. During her first semester at Chicago’s Malcolm X College, Nikya Harrell had had enough. It was winter, and she was cold. She was bouncing to and from family members’ houses and sometimes could only afford one meal a week. Harrell came to school overwhelmed and crying. A concerned friend suggested she see the school’s therapist, who connected her with the Dax Program, which offers students at risk of or experiencing homelessness a place to live for up to two years. Harrell came to Denver for Depaul USA’s Dax Program’s recent opening of the city’s first student residence near the Capitol building. Harrell had a message for other students who face challenges finding a place to live that she’s often repeated to herself: “You’re never alone.” Community members gather to bless the newly opened Depaul USA Dax Program housing on September 24, 2026, in Denver. Credit: Jason Gonzales / Chalkbeat Dax provides students with a safe living space that allows them to focus on getting a college degree without worrying about where they’ll sleep. The program has partnered with Metropolitan State University of Denver and Regis University, but wants to expand services to other local colleges and universities. The nonprofit provides resources to people experiencing homelessness and operates 11 Dax student housing programs in Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and New York. The program started in 2015 and has housed 494 students in those cities. The Denver Dax residence, an 1890s brick building that was originally a duplex in North Capitol Hill, is one of the national program’s larger residences and will be able to house up to 15 students. headline_hi: हल्दी की खेती से बचाई फसल
summary_en: In Uttar Pradesh's Terai Elephant Reserve, farmers and conservationists are together conducting a new experiment. Farmers here grow paddy, maize, and sugarcane. Elephants like these crops because they provide them with plenty of energy. But crop damage can wipe out months of hard work and all the earnings of the farmers. Now, 100 farmers are trying to plant turmeric alongside these crops. Elephants are less attracted to turmeric compared to paddy, maize, or sugarcane. Therefore, farmers are being encouraged to plant turmeric. This experiment will succeed only if turmeric grows well, farming costs remain low, and it gets a fair price in the market. This reserve spans an area of more than 3,000 square kilometers, and farmers are trying to protect their livelihoods.

lead.title: Why 100 UP Farmers Are Planting Turmeric Beside Crops That Elephants Love to Eat
lead.summary: For a farmer, a field of paddy or sugarcane is months of work standing in one place. If elephants enter and damage the crop, a season’s income can disappear with it. For an elephant moving through the Terai, the same field looks very different. Paddy, maize and sugarcane are all food, and they offer plenty of energy in a relatively small area. This overlap between what a farmer depends on and what an elephant wants to eat lies at the centre of a difficult question: how do you protect livelihoods in a landscape elephants continue to use? Fences are one answer. In parts of Uttar Pradesh’s Terai Elephant Reserve, farmers and conservationists are also trying something else. They are looking at what grows inside the field. The crop drawing attention is turmeric, which elephants are less attracted to than paddy, maize or sugarcane. Farmers are being encouraged to grow it alongside, or in place of some of, the crops that are more vulnerable to elephant damage. The idea makes sense only if it works for the farmer too. Turmeric has to grow well, cost less to cultivate and find a market that pays enough to make the shift worthwhile. That is where this experiment begins. Why are elephants choosing farms over forests? The Terai Elephant Reserve was notified in December 2022 and covers more than 3,000 sq km across the Dudhwa-Pilibhit landscape. It includes forest areas associated with Dudhwa, Pilibhit, Katarniaghat and Kishanpur. Government sources put Uttar Pradesh’s elephant population at about 232. The reserve also borders Nepal, and elephants move across the international boundary. Their route, however, does not run through one continuous stretch of forest. headline_hi: रसोई के मसालों से बढ़ेगी इम्यूनिटी
summary_en: Common spices from our kitchen are proving to be very beneficial for health. Many important findings have emerged from research by scientists at the New York Institute. Compounds in turmeric, ginger, garlic, and basil strengthen our immune system. They have a natural ability to reduce inflammation in the body and fight bacteria. Curcumin, found in turmeric, gives new strength to immune cells. According to Dr. Mindy Haar, this compound activates the body's T cells. But our body cannot fully absorb curcumin on its own. The simple solution to this is to add a pinch of black pepper with turmeric. The piperine in black pepper helps deliver curcumin directly into the bloodstream. Taking this combination in warm soup or milk protects against seasonal illnesses. This small change in our daily diet can keep all of us healthy throughout the year.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: The herbs and spices dietitians say support immune function
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, the same conversation starts about how to stay well through cold and flu season. Most of the advice points to supplements: vitamin C, zinc, elderberry. Useful, but not the whole picture. The spice rack you walk past every morning has something to say about immunity too, and the research behind it is more substantial than most people expect. Six common herbs and spices- turmeric, garlic, ginger, oregano, basil, and rosemary- contain bioactive compounds that support immune function through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects. They are not replacements for sleep, exercise, or a balanced diet, but as a regular part of how you cook, they do real work. Here is what registered dietitians say about each one. Turmeric Turmeric’s immune benefits come down to curcumin, its main active compound. “Curcumin promotes the health of T cells, B cells, and macrophages, the cells your immune system uses to fight germs and other threats,” says Mindy Haar , Ph.D., R.D.N., department chair of interdisciplinary health science at the New York Institute of Technology’s School of Health Professions. Haar also notes that curcumin “lowers the activity of proteins that trigger the production of inflammatory chemicals in the body,” which matters because chronic inflammation raises the risk of illness. The catch is that the body does not absorb curcumin well on its own. Haar’s fix is simple: combine turmeric with a small amount of black pepper, roughly one-eighth to one-quarter teaspoon. Black pepper contains piperine, which slows curcumin’s breakdown in the digestive system and allows more to reach the bloodstream.
